content: Aniline, also known as phenylamine or aminobenzene, is an organic compound with the chemical formula C6H5NH2. It is the simplest aromatic amine and serves as a precursor for the synthesis of more complex chemicals. Its primary industrial application is in the production of polyurethane. Aniline has a characteristic unpleasant odor reminiscent of rotten fish and a burning aromatic taste. It is highly toxic and acrid. The compound is flammable and burns with a smoky flame. Structurally, aniline consists of a phenyl group attached to an amino group. Industrially, it is synthesized in two steps starting from benzene. First, benzene is nitrated using a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at temperatures between 50–60°C. This process generates the electrophile NO2+, which reacts with benzene, replacing a proton (H+) on the aromatic ring to form nitrobenzene. In the second step, nitrobenzene is hydrogenated at approximately 600°C in the presence of a nickel catalyst, yielding aniline. This process is known as hydrogenation. Numerous derivatives of aniline can be synthesized using similar methods. Commercially, three grades of aniline are recognized: aniline oil for blue, which is pure aniline; aniline oil for red, a mixture of aniline and orthoand para-toluidines in equimolar proportions; and aniline oil for safranine, which contains aniline and ortho-toluidine and is obtained from the distillate of fuchsine fusion. Aniline is a colorless liquid but gradually oxidizes and resinifies when exposed to air, resulting in a red-brown tint in aged samples. Its oxidation has been extensively studied. In alkaline solutions, it forms azobenzene, while arsenic acid produces violaniline, a violet-colored compound. Chromic acid oxidizes aniline to quinone, and chlorates in the presence of certain metallic salts, particularly vanadium, yield aniline black. Hydrochloric acid and potassium chlorate produce chloranil. Potassium permanganate oxidizes aniline to nitrobenzene in neutral solutions, azobenzene, ammonia, and oxalic acid in alkaline solutions, and aniline black in acidic solutions. Hypochlorous acid reacts with aniline to form 4-aminophenol and para-amino diphenylamine. Aniline is a weak base. Aromatic amines like aniline are generally weaker bases than aliphatic amines. When reacted with strong acids, aniline forms the anilinium ion (C6H5-NH3+), and its sulfate salt crystallizes as white plates. Despite its weak basicity, aniline precipitates zinc, aluminum, and ferric salts and releases ammonia from its salts upon heating. Aniline reacts with carboxylic acids or, more readily, with acyl chlorides such as acetyl chloride to form amides. These amides are sometimes referred to as anilides. For example, acetanilide (CH3-CO-NH-C6H5) is formed from acetic acid and aniline. Acetanilide, also known as antifebrin, was historically used as a medication. Aniline reacts directly with alkyl iodides to produce secondary and tertiary amines. Monomethyl and dimethyl aniline are colorless liquids prepared by heating aniline, aniline hydrochloride, and methyl alcohol in an autoclave at 220°C. These compounds are significant in the dye industry. Monomethyl aniline has a boiling point of 193–195°C, while dimethyl aniline boils at 192°C. When boiled with carbon disulfide, aniline forms sulfocarbanylide (diphenyl thiourea), which can decompose into phenyl isothiocyanate and triphenyl guanidine. Like phenols, aniline derivatives are highly reactive in electrophilic substitution reactions. For instance, sulfonation of aniline produces sulfanilic acid, which can be converted into sulfanilamide. Sulfanilamide is one of the sulfa drugs that were widely used as antibacterials in the early 20th century. Reaction with sulfuric acid at 180°C also produces sulfanilic acid (NH2C6H4SO3H). Aniline and its ring-substituted derivatives react with nitrous acid to form diazonium salts. These salts allow the amino group (-NH2) of aniline to be conveniently converted into hydroxyl (-OH), cyano (-CN), or halide groups via Sandmeyer reactions. Aniline reacts with nitrobenzene in the Wohl-Aue reaction to produce phenazine. Historically, aniline's commercial value was initially tied to its ability to produce dyes. The discovery of mauveine, the first synthetic dye, by William Henry Perkin in 1856 marked the beginning of the synthetic dye industry. Aniline was originally an expensive laboratory compound but became widely available after Antoine Béchamp developed a scalable production process. The dye industry rapidly expanded in the late 1850s and 1860s with the discovery of new aniline-based dyes. Aniline derivatives, such as p-toluidine, are also used in qualitative analysis to prepare carboxylic acid derivatives. Aniline is toxic when inhaled, absorbed through the skin, or ingested. Acute exposure can cause symptoms such as headache, drowsiness, cyanosis, mental confusion, and, in severe cases, convulsions. Prolonged exposure affects the nervous system and blood, leading to fatigue, loss of appetite, headache, and dizziness. Epidemiological and chemical studies have linked mixtures containing aniline, such as rapeseed oil denatured with aniline, to the toxic oil syndrome epidemic in Spain in 1981, which caused over 20,000 acute illnesses, 12,000 hospitalizations, and more than 350 deaths in the first year. The exact etiology of this syndrome remains unclear. Some authorities classify aniline as a carcinogen, although the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) lists it as Group 3 (not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans) due to limited and contradictory data.
